author: ziiizar
body:
## Resumen

Dos bloques de trabajo sobre la misma rama.

**La home, rehecha** sobre la variante D2 del banco de exploraciones: cambia el
sujeto del comparador (ya no enfrenta kits entre sí, sino proveedores del mismo
kit), el buscador se monta a caballo del borde de la foto y funciona como
pestañas, y la página cierra en dos bloques de tinta. Arrastra una recalibración
del design system y **el arreglo de un fallo mudo de `cn()`** que borraba
colores en todo el proyecto.

**La instalación como servicio**, cerrada de punta a punta —tabla propia,
carrito, catálogo y ficha— y la **ficha de producto/kit/servicio** rehecha a dos
columnas con tres regiones que no se empujan entre sí. Más un tratamiento de
foto que hace que el catálogo se lea como una pieza impresa y no como un tablón
de fotos de proveedores distintos.

---

## Principales cambios / diferencias

### 1 · La home sobre el D2

La página pasa a estar en el orden en que se decide una compra: qué necesitas,
quién te lo instala, dónde llega, de quién te fías, y solo al final el otro
interlocutor y las dudas.

- **El comparador cambia de sujeto.** Ya no enfrenta tres kits entre sí —eso lo
  elige el buscador del hero— sino proveedores del mismo kit, que es la pregunta
  que queda cuando ya sabes cuál te hace falta.
- **El buscador desborda el hero.** Va montado a caballo del borde inferior de
  la foto: es lo que impide que el hero se lea como un cartel cerrado y la
  página como otra cosa que empieza después. Sus tres kits son **pestañas**, no
  enlaces — cambian el contenido de la sección de abajo sin navegar ni pedir
  nada, porque las ofertas de los tres llegan con la página y viven en un
  contexto de cliente.
- **La sección de confianza** deja de ser una lista y pasa a ser un solo bloque
  de tinta con las piezas separadas por un pelo: los filetes no son bordes, es
  el material asomando por las juntas, y por eso casan entre columnas de
  distinto alto.
- **El header** deja de flotar sobre la foto y de escuchar el scroll. Con la
  marca centrada, la transición dejaba la palabra sin apoyo sobre el cielo;
  ahora es una barra sólida con su filete. Al salir el `useEffect` vuelve a ser
  componente de servidor. Afecta también al catálogo, que lo comparte.
- **La banda de proveedores** esconde el formulario tras el botón: en reposo es
  un argumento, que es lo que pide quien todavía no sabe si esto va con él.
- FAQ nuevo, centrado, y **pie a sangre** con la marca recortada por los dos
  bordes del viewport.
- El **mapa se queda como estaba**: estructura y pieza siguen siendo buenas.

### 2 · Design system

- **Escala de titulares** recalibrada a 64 / 44 / 40 / 32 / 28 / 24. Los `vw` de
  cada `clamp` caen clavados en el tope a 1440px, el ancho al que está dibujada
  la home: el desktop coincide con el boceto y por debajo la escala baja sola,
  sin un solo breakpoint.
- **`--canvas` deja el verde y se muda a la tinta.** La página cierra con dos
  bloques oscuros seguidos —proveedores y pie— y en verde competían con el
  acento; en tinta, el único color de esas dos secciones es el botón. Afecta a
  las exploraciones de `/design`, que comparten el rol.
- **`--primary-loud`** pasa a ser el acento de la home y no solo de una
  exploración, y su foreground es **blanco puro**: el hueso del resto del
  sistema se ensucia sobre un naranja de esta saturación.
- **`--scrim-hero`** solo pesa abajo, y se registra como utilidad
  (`bg-scrim-hero`) para no llamarlo por `style` inline.
- Roles nuevos: `text-brand`, `text-body-xs`, `text-micro`,
  `--spacing-section-lg` y cuatro peldaños de tracking mono.

### 3 · `cn()` borraba colores en silencio — ojo a esto al revisar

`text-` es ambiguo en Tailwind: vale para el color (`text-foreground`) y para el
tamaño (`text-display-1`). tailwind-merge solo reconoce como tamaño los sufijos
de la escala de Tailwind, así que daba los roles de este proyecto por colores y
al fusionar borraba el anterior por repetido:

```
cn("text-primary-loud-foreground", "text-data")  ->  "text-data"
```

El elemento se quedaba heredando el color del body. **Es un fallo mudo**: la
clase desaparece del HTML, no hay error de build ni de lint, y afectaba a todo
el proyecto —no a una pantalla— siempre que un color fuera antes de un rol de
tamaño dentro del mismo `cn()`. Se veía como botones del mismo tono con la
tipografía de dos colores distintos, según si la clase pasaba por `cn()` o iba
escrita en un literal.

Los roles se declaran ahora en `TEXT_ROLES` (`lib/utils.ts`) y alimentan un
`extendTailwindMerge`: dos tamaños se siguen pisando entre sí, dos colores
también, y un tamaño y un color ya no se tocan. **`check:tokens` compara
`TEXT_ROLES` con los `--text-*` del `@theme` y falla si se desincronizan**, que
es la única forma de que esto vuelva.

### 4 · Instalación como servicio (BD → carrito → catálogo)

- Tres tablas nuevas: `services` (precio `FLAT` o `PER_UNIT` con su
  `unit_label`), `service_categories` (en tabla y no en enum: añadir
  "mantenimiento" no debería pedir un deploy) e `installation_offers` (qué
  instalación se ofrece con qué producto o kit). `order_item_type` suma
  `SERVICE`. **Migración `0002`.**
- Un servicio no es un producto: no tiene existencias ni entrega y su precio
  puede depender de la obra. Lo presta el mismo proveedor que vende, así que
  sigue valiendo la regla de un proveedor por orden y la cobertura ya sale de
  `supplier_zones`.
- Se vende de dos formas con el mismo modelo: **sola**, con ficha propia en
  `/catalog/services/[slug]`, o **añadida** desde la ficha del equipo que
  instala. Sin ofertas cargadas no se enseña el bloque.
- La línea de carrito pasa a `PurchasableType` y suma `unitLabel`.

### 5 · La ficha, rehecha

- Fotos a la izquierda con su propio scroll; a la derecha, tres regiones: la
  **cabecera fija** (qué es, cuánto cuesta, el botón), el **pie fijo** (hasta
  dónde llega el proveedor) y en medio lo único que se recorre.
- Las secciones se pliegan en un **acordeón**, una fila por cosa. Se separan por
  jerarquía de líneas y no por relleno: el pliegue entre filas es
  `border-border-strong` y todo filete de dentro queda un peldaño por debajo.
- La cobertura del proveedor **se mueve** (no se duplica) de la sección al pie:
  en este catálogo un equipo solo se compra si el proveedor opera donde vive
  quien mira, así que decide si el botón de arriba sirve de algo.
- Tira de **más de este proveedor** (`getSupplierRelated`): `UNION ALL` de kits
  y productos ordenado y cortado por Postgres. Del mismo proveedor porque una
  orden la entrega uno solo — es lo único que cabe en el mismo carrito.
- La salida al catálogo pasa a flotar sobre las fotos, hermana de la tira y no
  hija, para que no se mueva con su scroll.
- El acordeón se monta sobre el primitivo de Radix del paquete `radix-ui` que ya
  estaba, no con `npx shadcn add`: así no entra un icono de lucide que habría
  que migrar y `components/ui/` sigue siendo solo código del CLI.
- Se van `catalog-gallery.tsx` y `catalog-purchase-panel.tsx`.

### 6 · Duotono de las fotos del catálogo

- `CatalogMedia` gana `duotone`: dos capas de mezcla imprimen la foto en la
  paleta. `--photo-highlight` recorta las altas luces al papel de la ficha —el
  fondo blanco de estudio desaparece y el producto queda impreso sobre la hoja—
  y `--photo-shadow` levanta los negros a un verde de la familia del lienzo.
- La capa del papel se queda siempre, también en táctil: recortar altas luces no
  le quita color a un producto. El duotono completo solo se monta donde hay
  cursor para deshacerlo (`pointer-fine`), y el hover devuelve el color real sin
  que vuelva el recuadro blanco.
- El acento terracota no entra: es el color de la acción, y una pared de fotos
  en terracota lo dejaría sin significar nada.

### 7 · Banco de exploraciones

- Cuatro exploraciones completas de la home en `/design` (terroir, workshop,
  media y **bois-franc**, la que se ha implementado) y el pie que se destapa al
  subir la página como

author: johnnymo87
body:
W3 of the scheduled-swarm-wake roadmap. Tracked as `pigeon-346`; spine is `pigeon-mx2`. Independent of W1/W2.

## The problem

The delivery watchdog verifies a handoff by looking for an assistant run in the target's transcript, and escalates when it doesn't find one: requeue, then abort-and-redeliver, then fail and notify the sender.

**That ladder is invalid against idle targets.** `pigeon-3m5` (open P1, observed live 2026-07-25): a send to a registered-but-idle session had `handed_off_at` advance while `verified_at` stayed null. The watchdog requeued, then aborted and redelivered. The target received **two identical envelopes**, and the sender was told the message "was NOT received." Verification requires the target to actually *process* the prompt, which an idle session may not do promptly — so non-verification is not a liveness proof for idle targets.

A woken session is idle **by definition** — it has been asleep for hours. So `pigeon-3m5` is this feature's *nominal* case, not an edge case. Every wake would produce duplicate turns plus a false failure report, and for a self-wake that report reaches the human, claiming a wake failed when it actually fired twice. That is worse than the silent drop this feature exists to fix; it is a *lying* drop.

**Abort is independently unacceptable.** A turn "silent" for `stuckAbortSilenceMs` (1h) can be a single long-running tool call — `lastActivityOf` only sees a part's `time.start` until the tool completes, so a 90-minute build qualifies. Wakes fire at scheduled times with no regard for target state, at hours nobody is watching, into exactly the long-horizon autonomous sessions most likely to be mid-build. The reminder destroys the work it came to check on.

## The change

For suppressed messages, `handed_off` (`prompt_async` returned 2xx) is **terminal success**. The watchdog still observes and alerts — that is useful signal — but never requeues and never aborts.

## Suppression follows the mechanism, not the label

The first cut of this keyed on `kind` matching `wake.*`. Adversarial review caught that this protects a *naming convention*, not the actual hazard: `POST /swarm/schedule` only **defaults** `kind` to `wake` and otherwise takes the caller's value verbatim. Scheduling with `kind: \"checkpoint\"` would walk straight back into the full ladder.

The invalid-liveness-proof argument applies to **every scheduled delivery** regardless of what the kind string says — a scheduled target is idle by definition. So suppression is now:

```ts
isWakeKind(row.kind) || row.deliverAt !== null
```

`deliver_at` is the mechanism and is already on the row the watchdog holds. The label remains as a secondary trigger so a caller can opt in without scheduling.

Near-misses fail **open** to existing behavior (`wakeup`, `awake`, `""` are not wake kinds, and there is a test). That is the safe direction: an ordinary message misnamed `wake.foo` loses redelivery, which is far less harmful than the duplicate-injection ladder.

## The alert covering the trade-off was backwards

We knowingly accept losing redelivery for the genuine "serve 2xx'd then died before processing" hole, with watchdog observation as the compensating control. Review found the one alert covering that hole was reassuring instead of warning: the `anchor === null` branch — where the prompt *never made it into the transcript*, so with requeue suppressed the wake will never fire — had copy-pasted text from the genuinely-idle branch saying it "remains unverified (expected for idle target)."

A silently lost wake plus a reassurance alert is worse than no alert. That branch now warns at severity `error` that the prompt was not found and the wake may be lost. The genuinely-idle branch keeps its original text.

## Also

- `requeueForRecovery` is now guarded `AND state = 'handed_off'` and returns whether it fired. It was safe only by accident — nothing currently transitions `handed_off -> cancelled/expired`, but that is an invariant held together at a distance. It joins the `terminal states are inescapable` matrix test. (This was a carried-forward finding from the W1 review.)
- `counts.requeued` no longer increments on a failed requeue.
- Corrected a doc comment that described a 7-day `cleanupOlderThan` retention sweep as if it ran. It does not — `swarm.cleanupOlderThan` has zero callers; only the outbox sweep is wired. Filed as `pigeon-755` rather than fixed here, to keep this change reviewable.

Note the consequence, since it is now load-bearing: suppressed rows stay `handed_off`/unverified, which keeps them eligible in `listUnverifiedHandedOff` indefinitely. Normal wakes exit within a cycle or two once revival runs a turn and `markVerified` fires. Perpetual residents are only genuinely-lost wakes and wakes to sessions whose 404 cannot be double-confirmed. Low rate, but monotonic — hence `pigeon-755`.

## Non-wake behavior is unchanged

All guards are purely additive early-returns; no existing branch condition, counter, or ordering moved. There is a positive-control test asserting `chat` and `task.assign` are still requeued when idle and still aborted when stuck, so an over-broad predicate breaks the suite.

The 404-confirmed-session-deleted path is deliberately left unsuppressed — the session genuinely no longer exists there, a different failure mode from the idle-target false negative, and it is the only exit that evicts dead-session rows.

## Testing

986 daemon tests (1,584 workspace-wide), typecheck clean. Headline test is the `pigeon-3m5` shape as a regression: a wake to an idle target across multiple cycles is never requeued, the row stays `handed_off`, and no failure notification fires. All suppression guards including the two previously-untested branches (`anchor === null`, pre-existing `abortedAt`) have coverage, and each new test was confirmed to fail before its fix.

## Relationship to pigeon-3m5

Decoupled, **not** blocked. If `pigeon-3m5` is fixed — giving verification semantics valid for idle targets — revisit and consider re-enabling recovery for wakes.

author: bovarafa
body:
## What changed
Two complementary form-integrity fixes coming out of the Edit-functionality review (Branches Unit/Country reported empty on edit):

### 1. Edit drawer lost cascaded selections — and wiped them on save
The edit-mode prefill runs per field, but the initial cascade pass fires afterwards and `fillOptions` rebuilt each cascaded select **without restoring its value**. Beyond display: `commit()` collects every control, so opening an Edit drawer and saving untouched **erased the stored FK** (e.g. a Branch lost `businessUnitID` and `countryName`). `applyOpts` now preserves the selection across refills — the same pattern `mkMultiCheck`/`mkRadioList`/`certified-responsible` already implemented; the generic select path was the only one missing it. **25 single-select cascade fields across 7 modules** were affected (People, Onboarding, Competence, Events, Processes, Jobs, Customers, Scopes, Requirements, Forecast Scopes, Workflows…).

### 2. NOT NULL anchors (approved list)
45 constraint marks in `datamodel.json` on structural anchors — cascade deps and derived-chain join keys — since a null anchor makes a record invisible to every derived chain (the anatomy of all recent bugs). Enforcement:
- **Form engine** — `requiredAttrs()` (NOT NULL attrs + the table's label attr, enforced generically) and `missingRequired()`; `commit()` blocks the save with a toast listing the empty fields; required labels get a `*` (display-only — cascade/check lookups keep undecorated keys). Only form-control attrs are enforced: derived-on-save keys (`Competence.departmentID`) and by-design nullables (Q1 wildcard applicability on Requirements, `parentStepID`, `People.squadID/branchID`, `Processes.squadID`) stay out.
- **Validator** — new `== required fields (NOT NULL) ==` section in `validate_mockup.py`, failing (not warning) on seed violations.
- **Seeds** — `migrate_required_seeds.py` backfills the three legacy gaps found: Scopes C/D/E/F take their opportunity issue's units, A.4 falls back to the A.* prefix family, Functions F6 "Manager" (no people, no derivable source) takes BU01 by the first-unit convention.
- **List adjustment** — `Activities.processID` was dropped from the approved list: the current model links activities through Workflows, not a stored FK.

**Tests** — new `test_engine_required.mjs` (13 assertions: anchors + label rule, nullable-by-design exemptions, commit gate with null/`''`/empty-list, full-seed sweep). All **10 suites** green; `validate_mockup.py` PASS (0 failures). The select-value preservation is real-DOM behavior the node suites can't cover — manual check: edit a Branch (Unit/Country prefilled, `*` markers visible), save untouched (values persist), and try saving a new record with a required field empty (blocked with the toast).

- [x] fix (edit-drawer data loss) + data (NOT NULL constraints + seed backfill)

author: digant73
body:
**AI Disclosure:**
- Primary target of the PR is to identify the regressing code (reporting the PR and and possibly the regressing commit when possible) so it can help main developers to provide a correct fix in case the one provided by AI is not fully applicable.
- Comments on the code provided by AI are not initially removed just to provide main developers a description of the changes. Comments will be removed/changed as per indication from main developers during the review
- Analysis made by Opus 5
- Testers needed on #15373 and #15410

</br>

Fix regression introduced by the PR https://github.com/RPCS3/rpcs3/pull/15364). The regression was introduced in commit [vm: Fix writer lock leak](https://github.com/RPCS3/rpcs3/pull/15364/commits/37dc40277f25e3e35058bf76687d12e17fabc5fc).

This PR should fix that regression.

</br>

(to be tested) probably fixes #15410
(to be tested) probably fixes #15373

</br>

**NOTE:** marking the PR as draft for review from elad335

</br>

### AI Summary

**The bug**

Introduced by 8588b2b11 "vm: Fix writer lock leak" (2024-03-27), the only commit in the given range that touches the code path gated by Accurate PPU 128 Reservations.

That commit legitimately fixed a lock leak (acquire path and destructor disagreed on which lock had been taken), but in doing so it changed two other semantics:

1. vm.cpp — the gate for the "suspend all PPU threads" phase went from if (addr >= 0x10000) to if (range_lock). Callers passing no range lock (vm::reservation_op,
  do_cell_atomic_128_store outside SPU threads) silently lost the stop-the-world, despite performing non-atomic 128-byte stores.
2. PPUThread.cpp — the PPU 128-byte stdcx path was switched from the global exclusive lock to a per-slot range lock.

Change 2 is what freezes the game. Per-slot exclusive locks do not exclude each other — the drain loop explicitly skips slots already marked exclusive (to_clear & ~get_range_lock_bits(true)). So:

- An SPU in do_putllc enters its writer_lock suspend phase and, for every PPU that already has cpu_flag::wait, skips setting cpu_flag::memory.
- A PPU entering its accurate stdcx sets cpu_flag::wait in the lock constructor — so the SPU sees it as parked and moves on without marking it.
- The PPU then acquires its own slot immediately (previously it would have blocked, holding wait the whole time), and at the and of the constructor does state -= cpu_flag::memory + cpu_flag::wait — it unparks itself and returns to guest code.
- The SPU's second wait loop now waits for that PPU forever: nothing will ever set cpu_flag::memory on it. If the PPU is spinning in guest code on the value the SPU is about to write, it's a hard deadlock, with the SPU still holding the reservation lock and its bit in g_range_lock_bits[1].

With the option Disabled the PPU never takes a range-lock-based writer_lock during guest execution, so the window doesn't exist — matching the reported symptom.

</br>

**The fix**

Two files, restoring pre-8588b2b11 semantics while keeping the actual leak fix (the acquire gate if (!range_lock) is untouched, so acquire and destructor stay coherent):

- rpcs3/Emu/Memory/vm.cpp:528 — suspend gate becomes range_lock || addr >= 0x10000, restoring the stop-the-world for vm::reservation_op and for do_cell_atomic_128_store called outside SPU threads.
- rpcs3/Emu/Cell/PPUThread.cpp:3262 — the 128-byte path goes back to the global vm::writer_lock lock(addr); alloc_range_lock/free_range_lock removed (they also burned one of the 63 slots on every stdcx).

</br>

**Performance**

The only cost is the performance overhead that existed before March 2024 (global serialization of PPU 128-byte atomics, PPU suspension in cellSpurs HLE reservation ops, and dcbz only when Accurate Cache Line Stores is on) — worth an A/B benchmark, but not a behavioral regression.

release record against a zip built from this tree. That settles record against tree. Nothing
settled deployed against record: AWS reports the running code as `CodeSha256`, and until now
nothing read it outside a maintainer doing it by hand.

A function deployed out of band, a release recorded from a tree that did not build it, or two
releasers racing all leave CI green over an account running code `main` does not describe. On
2026-08-01 two `release_lambdas=true` dispatches ran minutes apart from the same account,
harmless only because both built from the same commit. The concurrency group queues releases;
it does not stop the second releaser recording the first one's digest.

## The change

`tools/verify_deployed_lambdas.py` reads each release record, calls
`lambda:GetFunctionConfiguration`, decodes `CodeSha256` to hex and compares. It reports every
function rather than stopping at the first, and separates the two ways of being non-zero
because they send a reader to different places:

| Exit | Reason | What it means |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | | every function checked is running what its record describes |
| 1 | `deployed_lambda_is_not_the_release` | the digests disagree |
| 1 | `deployed_lambda_absent` | no such function; nothing is deployed |
| 2 | `deployed_lambda_unreadable` | the call failed, so nothing was read |
| 2 | `release_record_unusable`, `lambda_template_unusable` | the local inputs could not be read |

A mismatch outranks an unanswered question in the exit code, and both are printed.

The function names are read from the templates that declare them to CloudFormation rather
than spelled in the tool, and the function table is `release_lambda.FUNCTIONS`, so a third
Lambda is covered from the day it can be released.

Only the AWS error code is repeated on a failure. An `AccessDenied` from Lambda names the
calling and resource ARNs and both carry the account id, and this runs in a scheduled job
whose log and step summary are public.

## S3ObjectVersion: separate, and it already exists

Not folded in. The template-against-record comparison is between two committed files and is
already made once per function, by
`test_the_template_pins_the_object_the_release_record_names` and
`test_the_template_and_the_record_name_the_same_object`. Those need no AWS identity and fail
on the pull request that causes the drift; moving or duplicating the property would put it on
a schedule and in two places, which is the arrangement `test_phase3_lifecycle_package.py`
argues against in its own docstring.

Lambda could not contribute to it in any case. `GetFunctionConfiguration` reports the digest
of the deployed code, not the S3 object version it was deployed from, so deployed-against-
record has no object-version half. The digest is the stronger question because it is about
the bytes rather than a pointer to them.

`test_the_object_version_comparison_is_owned_by_the_release_tripwires` reads both citations,
so deleting or renaming them leaves nothing making the comparison and fails here.

## The grant

`infra/iam/nightly-reader-role.yaml` gains `lambda:GetFunctionConfiguration` on the two
function ARNs, named rather than wildcarded, as two statements. Applied from a laptop with the
command in `infra/README.md`. `iam simulate-principal-policy` on the deployed role:

| Action | admission-validator | lifecycle-recorder |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `lambda:GetFunctionConfiguration` | allowed | allowed |
| `lambda:UpdateFunctionCode` | implicitDeny | implicitDeny |
| `lambda:GetFunction` | implicitDeny | implicitDeny |
| `lambda:ListFunctions` | implicitDeny | implicitDeny |

`GetFunctionConfiguration` on `…:function:sbsandbox-intern-edullm-admission-validator-copy` is
also `implicitDeny`, so the ARNs are exact and not name prefixes. The adjacent action is the
one worth simulating: a check that could deploy could answer its own finding by making the
account match the record.

## Evidence

Run against the account, verbatim, with `infra/lifecycle-recorder-release.yaml` temporarily
edited to a wrong digest:

```
sbsandbox-intern-edullm-admission-validator is running e0e420a5cdba, which is what infra/admission-validator-release.yaml records.
deployed_lambda_is_not_the_release
sbsandbox-intern-edullm-lifecycle-recorder is running 99c0223a989f8b2816697804a82367ab911714a3de553092c9ea65b2dd97ab02 and infra/lifecycle-recorder-release.yaml records deadbeef989f8b2816697804a82367ab911714a3de553092c9ea65b2dd97ab02, so the account is running code this tree does not describe. Which side is out of step is what tests/test_phase3_lifecycle_package.py answers: it holds the record against a zip built from this tree, so while it is green the record still describes the tree and the account is the side to look at -- either something was deployed out of band, or the deploy this record was cut for has not landed yet, which CI does when the edited template reaches main.
```

Exit 1. The perturbation was reverted; the tree is clean. With a renamed function in the
template the same run reports `deployed_lambda_absent` and exits 1; with no credentials it
reports `deployed_lambda_unreadable` and exits 2.

Against the account as it stands, both functions agree and the tool exits 0. It followed the
release recorded in #163 through without an edit, which is what reading the records rather
than pinning digests buys.

## Notes

- `release_lambda.Function` gains the `tripwire` path it was previously matching on by display
  name. `verify` now reads it, and the verifier cites the right module per function.
- The job is red in the minutes between a record-cut PR merging and CI deploying the template.
  The nightly runs once a day, so this is a caveat for a hand dispatch after a release; the
  failure names both digests, so the case is recognisable.
- `tests/test_workflow_tool_arguments.py::…[nightly.yml:tools/find_runs_that_saved_nothing.py]`
  fails when that module is selected alone, on `main` as well as here. It passes in the full
  suite because another module imports the tool first. Pre-existing and untouched.

`uv run pytest -q`: 4190 passed, 124 skipped. `ruff check .` and `mypy` clean.

body:
## Summary

Follow-up sweep on #1795 (the 70h public-record anchoring outage). That PR repointed `fetchAnchorRows` and `claimPendingPipelineAnchors` at `POSTGREST_IN_FILTER_CHUNK`. **Two more `.in()` sites in the same family were left unfixed** — one of them in the main customer anchoring drain.

### 1. `revertClaimedAnchors` (`publicRecordAnchor.ts`) — the rollback path

The compensating write that returns claimed anchors from `BROADCASTING` to `PENDING` when `submitFingerprint` throws was still chunking by `POSTGREST_ROW_LIMIT` (1,000). At 1,000 UUIDs the encoded `in.(...)` value is ~38 KB, PostgREST answers `400 Bad Request`, and the loop only logs and continues — so the entire rollback no-ops.

**Blast radius is a stall, not data loss.** `recover_stuck_broadcasts` (migration `0358`) resets any anchor with `status='BROADCASTING' AND chain_tx_id IS NULL AND deleted_at IS NULL`, no `PENDING`/`HELD` `anchor_txid_journal` row, and a stale `updated_at` (default 5 min). Anchors claimed by this job match every predicate — it writes no journal row and never sets `chain_tx_id` on the failure path. Until that pass runs the batch is head-of-line blocked: `batch_insert_anchors` returns the same oldest-first records, `partitionRecordAnchors` buckets the `BROADCASTING` rows nowhere, and the job reports "no new pending" with HTTP 200.

> An earlier revision of this PR described the cohort as permanently stranded and needing manual recovery. That was wrong, and it is corrected in the code comments, the log line, `agents.md`, and the test. Flagged by both review passes.

### 2. `batch-anchor.ts` CML-02 `compliance_controls` back-fill — same bug, customer path

Unchunked `.in('id', ids)` where `ids` is a per-credential-type group of `orderedAnchors`, bounded only by `BATCH_SIZE` (**10,000**). Real batches concentrate in a few credential types, so this is a ~390 KB query string that PostgREST 400s. It sits inside a non-fatal `try/catch` that only warns, so the symptom is silent: **large batches received no `compliance_controls` at all**, and the throw skipped every remaining credential type. Downstream (`audit-export`, GRC evidence) just emits empty control lists.

Now chunked with per-chunk error capture, so one bad chunk cannot cancel the rest.

### Also

- `revertClaimedAnchors` returns `{ attempted, failed }` and the caller logs `revertFailed` alongside the chain error. The previous `reverted` count claimed to be an affected-row count, which the call structurally cannot know (no `.select()`, and `.eq('status','BROADCASTING')` can legitimately match fewer rows).
- The aggregate failure line is documented as a log **event**, not an alert — `utils/logger.ts` is plain pino to stdout with no Sentry transport and no log-based metric references it. Same `event != alert` distinction the repo already draws for SCRUM-2902.
- Corrected the `POSTGREST_IN_FILTER_CHUNK` byte comment: a UUID costs ~39 encoded bytes (the comma expands to `%2C`), not 37. 200 ids = 7,802 B against the 8,192 B budget, so 210 already lands on the ceiling.
- `agents.md` no longer contradicts itself on chunk width — the rule is "`POSTGREST_IN_FILTER_CHUNK` (200) **or smaller**", which makes the pre-existing 100-id chunkers correct as-is.

### Same-class audit — known remaining sites, out of scope here

Listed in `agents.md` so they don't get lost:

| Site | Bound on the id array |
|---|---|
| `api/v1/auditBatchVerify.ts` | unbounded |
| `billing/meteredBilling.ts` | unbounded (fails **closed** — metered billing silently stops) |
| `api/v1/anchor-bulk.ts` | 1,000 sha256 hex (over budget past ~120) |
| `jobs/trainingExporter.ts`, `api/v1/directory-opt-out.ts` | 1,000 |
| `utils/pipeline.ts` `getExistingSourceIds` | ~40 (bounded by hardcoded statute defs), but ignores `error` entirely |

Legitimate `POSTGREST_ROW_LIMIT` uses confirmed unchanged: `publicRecordAnchor.ts` `.range()` offset loops, `batch-anchor.ts` claim-RPC row cap.

## 2026-08-02 update — superseded-in-place by #1839/#1845, merge-resolved onto main

#1839 (`chunkForInFilter`/`utils/postgrest-filter.ts`) and #1845 (`applyComplianceControls`
extraction) merged to `main` ahead of this PR and independently fixed both defects described above —
`revertClaimedAnchors`' chunking and the CML-02 back-fill — with a more complete version of the same
fix (caller-owned aggregate escalation, per-chunk error-level logging naming `unstampedAnchors`,
`chunkForInFilter`'s byte-budget-aware width instead of a hand-rolled `i += SIZE` loop). Merge
resolution took **main's implementation in both spots** rather than reintroducing this PR's
hand-rolled version — main's code already is this PR's fix, refined.

This PR's own two regression tests were rebased onto the surviving APIs rather than dropped:
- `publicRecordAnchor-revert-in-filter.test.ts` — import repointed at `utils/postgrest-filter.js`
  (the constant's new home). Kept as real-entrypoint (`processPublicRecordAnchoring`) coverage of
  chunk accounting at multi-chunk scale (607 real UUID-shaped ids) — neither the helper's own tests
  nor `publicRecordAnchor.test.ts`'s "claim-revert escalation" describe block exercise that scale
  through the real function. Its second test (chunk-failure escalation) was dropped: it asserted on
  log text main already replaced, and the behavior is already covered, more precisely, in
  `publicRecordAnchor.test.ts`.
- `batch-anchor.compliance-chunking.test.ts` — import repointed the same way. Kept as the
  real-entrypoint (`processBatchAnchors`) counterpart to #1845's unit-level
  `batch-anchor.compliance.test.ts` (which tests `applyComplianceControls` directly) — confirms the
  credential-type-grouping wiring at this specific call site.

Full detail in `services/worker/src/jobs/agents.md`.

## Soak tier

**T3** — `services/worker/src/jobs/batch-anchor.ts` classifies as anchor lifecycle / batch processor per the path detector (see prior correction below).

## Test plan

- [x] `publicRecordAnchor-revert-in-filter.test.ts` — chunk-width invariant through the real entrypoint, rebased onto `utils/postgrest-filter.js`.
- [x] `batch-anchor.compliance-chunking.test.ts` — chunk-width invariant through the real entrypoint, rebased onto `utils/postgrest-filter.js`.
- [x] `npx vitest run src/jobs/ src/routes/cron.test.ts` — 115 files passed, 2 skipped; 1762 tests passed, 7 skipped, 0 failed (2026-08-02, post-merge-resolution, real `npm ci` deps).

author: dankane2029
body:
Building has accumulated enough detail to be worth wrapping.

A viewer build needs two long arguments pointing CMake at development headers installed outside the system prefix. They're easy to leave out — and when you do, **the viewer silently disappears from the build** and everything still appears to work. That's the failure this exists to prevent.

```sh
scripts/build.sh                    # configure and build
scripts/build.sh --test             # ...and run the test suite
scripts/build.sh --clean --test     # ...from scratch
scripts/build.sh --debug            # debug build
scripts/build.sh --no-viewer        # headless only
```

It also fetches missing submodules, since cloning without `--recurse-submodules` is a common way to arrive at a build that can't work.

## A bug I introduced and caught

Each configuration builds into its own directory so switching doesn't force a rebuild. My first version set the name with three independent assignments:

```bash
BUILD_DIR="build"
[ "$BUILD_TYPE" = "Debug" ] && BUILD_DIR="build-debug"
[ "$VIEWER" -eq 0 ] && BUILD_DIR="build-headless"      # overwrites the line above
```

So `--debug --no-viewer` landed in `build-headless` — silently replacing a release build with a debug one, and forcing a full rebuild on every switch between them. The name is now composed rather than overwritten.

Verified all four combinations:

| Command | Directory |
| --- | --- |
| `build.sh` | `build` |
| `build.sh --no-viewer` | `build-headless` |
| `build.sh --debug` | `build-debug` |
| `build.sh --debug --no-viewer` | `build-debug-headless` |

Clean rebuild path exercised, 18 tests pass, and all four directories are already covered by the existing `build*/` ignore rule.

body:
## Summary
Complete rebrand from "Lumina Tech" (cyan/blue theme) to "Kyventis Tech" (deep amethyst purple + liquid copper theme), coupled with a migration from static HTML to a React-based component architecture. The site now features a modern design system with reusable components, improved accessibility, and a cohesive visual identity.

## Key Changes

### Branding & Design System
- **Color palette overhaul**: Replaced cyan (#06b6d4) and blue (#3b82f6) with deep amethyst (#2a1b4e, #120a24) and liquid copper (#e07a5f, #f0997e)
- **Typography**: Migrated from Space Grotesk to Plus Jakarta Sans (display) + Inter (body) + JetBrains Mono (code)
- **New design tokens**: Established `--color-amethyst`, `--color-copper`, `--color-alabaster` CSS variables with supporting utilities
- **Visual effects**: Added copper gradient text, liquid sheen animations, glass morphism panels, and floating orb backgrounds

### Architecture Migration
- **React components**: Converted static HTML pages into modular React components:
  - `Navbar.tsx` — Responsive navigation with scroll detection
  - `Hero.tsx` — Full-screen hero with ambient background and stats
  - `Services.tsx` — Six-service grid with icon cards
  - `Work.tsx` — Filterable project portfolio with category tags
  - `Studio.tsx` — Four-step process timeline
  - `Contact.tsx` — Form with validation and success state
  - `Footer.tsx` — Social links and company info
- **App.tsx**: Main entry point orchestrating all sections
- **Custom hook**: `useReveal()` for scroll-triggered animations via IntersectionObserver

### Styling & Utilities
- **New CSS layer** (`src/index.css`): Comprehensive design system with:
  - `.text-copper-gradient` and `.text-copper-liquid` for animated text
  - `.btn-liquid` with metallic sheen effect on hover
  - `.btn-ghost` outline button variant
  - `.glass` and `.glass-strong` backdrop blur panels
  - `.card-hover` elevation and border animations
  - `.reveal` scroll-in animation framework
  - Marquee, conic ring, and link underline utilities
- **Legacy style.css**: Updated with new color mappings and maintained backward compatibility

### Content & Metadata
- Updated all HTML page titles and favicons to reference Kyventis Tech
- Enhanced `index.html` with Open Graph meta tags and improved SEO metadata
- Replaced inline SVG favicon with PNG assets (`kyventis-mark.png`, `kyventis-logo.png`)

### Configuration
- **package.json**: Added React 19, React DOM, and Lucide React icons
- **vite.config.ts**: Integrated `@vitejs/plugin-react` for JSX support
- **tsconfig.json**: Enabled `"jsx": "react-jsx"` for automatic JSX transformation
- **firebase-applet-config.json**: Updated Firebase project credentials for Kyventis
- **server-app.ts**: Updated email sender name from "Lumina Tech" to "Kyventis Tech"

## Notable Implementation Details
- **Form validation**: Contact form includes real-time field validation with error states and touched tracking
- **Responsive design**: Mobile-first approach with Tailwind breakpoints; mobile menu toggle in navbar
- **Scroll animations**: Reveal animations trigger on intersection; navbar glass effect activates after scroll threshold
- **Accessibility**: Semantic HTML, ARIA labels, and keyboard-friendly navigation
- **Performance**: Lazy-loaded images, optimized animations with CSS transforms, and efficient event listeners with passive flags

author: experintellia
body:
From the 2026-08-01 security audit. Follow-up to #155, which fixed this for npm publishing and left the more user-facing half open.

## The problem

`deploy-pages.yml` is **production** (web.slothful.chat). It granted `contents: read`, `pages: write` and `id-token: write` at the *workflow* level to a `workflow_dispatch` on **any branch**, with none of the tag, version or main-ancestry verification `publish-npm.yml` grew in #155.

So a repository writer — or a compromised automation credential — could hand-deploy arbitrary unmerged code straight to production. #155 closed that door for the npm registry while leaving it open on the site users actually load.

## The fix

The gate moves into `.github/workflows/verify-release-tag.yml` as a reusable workflow, called as the first job by **both** `publish-npm.yml` and `deploy-pages.yml`. One file on purpose: two copies of a security gate drift, and a drifted gate is a hole. Net **−8 lines** across the two callers.

It proves the ref is a tag, that the tag still points where it did when the run started, that its commit is an ancestor of `main`, and that all four package versions match it.

Also in `deploy-pages.yml`:

- Top-level `permissions: {}`; each job takes only what it needs. **`id-token: write` — which mints the OIDC token that authenticates the prod deploy — now belongs to the `deploy` job alone**, which checks out nothing and runs no repository code. `build` keeps `pages: write` for `actions/configure-pages`; it cannot deploy on its own, and the gate means it only ever runs on a verified merged tag.
- The build checkout is pinned to `${{ github.sha }}` rather than the tag name, so a tag moved during the ~10-minute build can't ship something the gate never saw. Same fix as #155.

## One non-obvious detail

The caller has to hand the reusable workflow its `contents: read` grant explicitly. A called workflow can only ever *downgrade* the caller's token, so with top-level `permissions: {}` it would be capped at nothing and its own checkout would fail. Commented at both call sites.

## Verification

No Actions runner or actionlint here, so: all three workflows parse under `yaml.safe_load`, every `run:` block passes `bash -n`, and the resulting permission matrix is:

| workflow | job | permissions | gated |
|---|---|---|---|
| verify-release-tag | verify | `contents: read` | — |
| deploy-pages | verify-tag | `contents: read` | — |
| deploy-pages | build | `contents: read`, `pages: write` | `needs` + `ref_type == 'tag'` |
| deploy-pages | deploy | `pages: write`, `id-token: write` | `needs` + `ref_type == 'tag'` |
| publish-npm | verify-tag | `contents: read` | — |
| publish-npm | publish | `id-token: write`, `contents: write` | `needs` + `ref_type == 'tag'` |

No job holding deploy or publish privileges is reachable from a branch ref, by dispatch or otherwise.

**Worth a real check on the next release**, since neither can be exercised here: that the reusable-workflow permission handoff behaves as described, and that `actions/configure-pages` is content with job-scoped `pages: write`. Both fail loudly rather than silently if wrong.

## Still open from M-11

- **Release tags are unprotected.** The ancestry check means a forged tag can only point at a commit already on `main`, but a `v*` tag protection rule would close it properly. Repo-settings work, not code.
- **No release-wide concurrency group on `publish-npm.yml`**, so two overlapping releases can still finish out of order and move some packages' `latest` backwards. `deploy-pages.yml` has had a `pages` concurrency group all along.
- The active ruleset still targets only the default branch with zero required approvals and no required status checks.

## Summary
Surfaces the in-flight state of a disposition being delivered to a parked session: `deliverUndeliveredInboxItems` now emits a `session_feedback_pending` WS message (naming the session) before `sendOrResume` resolves, clears it once delivery concludes (success or failure), and the initial state burst replays it for clients that connect mid-window — so a resume-in-progress no longer looks dropped.

body:
Part of #49 (iteration 1 — profile seam and engine convergence). Paired with the counterpart PR in scikit-hep/hypothesis-awkward: scikit-hep/hypothesis-awkward#160.

## What

- The `.claude/skills/write-readme/SKILL.md` body becomes a repository-agnostic engine: values become profile references, one-repository machinery becomes conditional modules gated by the profile ("when the status dimension is enabled…", "when the section set is an output of the run…"), and parallel wordings unify.
- New `.claude/rules/persona-review-profile.md` carries every repository-specific fact under the 11 section headings the engine reads by name (Document, Personas, Declaration mechanism, Premise to pin, Sources, Fact-check targets, Status dimension, Verification, Record, Voice rules, Extra guidelines).
- New `.claude/rules/persona-review-engine.md`, path-scoped to the two files above, records the seam: the body is repository-agnostic and plugin-bound.
- The body is shared verbatim with scikit-hep/hypothesis-awkward's `write-docs-page` skill and is prettier-formatted, because that repository's pre-commit hook enforces prettier on Markdown.

## Definition of done (from #49)

- Mirror: the two `SKILL.md` bodies diff clean below the frontmatter, verified across the paired branches; the check against the counterpart's `main` holds once both PRs merge.
- Ledger: every deleted repository-specific line reappears in the profile, and shared machinery reappears generalized in the engine — nothing dropped, nothing invented.

author: sasisprite
body:
Completes Phase 3. Full results in [docs/PHASE3_VALIDATION.md](docs/PHASE3_VALIDATION.md).

## Password auth instead of Google OAuth

No Google Cloud project exists, and the rest of Phase 3 needs *an* identity, not specifically Google's. [ADR-0009](docs/adr/0009-password-auth-instead-of-google-oauth.md) records it.

**BL-013 now carries the OAuth migration requirements**, including the one that is easy to miss: a user who registered with a password and later signs in with Google on the same address must land on the *same* account. Getting that wrong silently creates a duplicate and the user loses their interests and subscription.

Protected endpoints resolve a `User` from a token and do not care how identity was established, so OAuth becomes an additional login route rather than a rewrite.

## Default credentials are the risk — so the guard is structural

Seeding known accounts is a well-understood vulnerability class, precisely because it is convenient in development and then survives into production. So:

- Passwords come from the environment; never committed, never logged, never printed by `bootstrap`
- `bootstrap` **never resets** an existing password — otherwise a routine command becomes a way to restore known credentials
- The app **refuses to start** outside `development` with a placeholder password or unset `JWT_SECRET`

It raises rather than warns, because a warning in a deploy log is not enforcement. Verified in all four states:

| Environment | Secrets | Result |
|---|---|---|
| development | all defaults | allowed (local work stays frictionless) |
| production | all defaults | **REFUSED**, naming all four problems |
| production | real secret + passwords, seeding off | allowed |
| production | JWT secret < 32 chars | **REFUSED** |

## Security details that are easy to get wrong

- **Login failures are byte-identical** whatever the cause, and an unknown email still burns a full Argon2 verification. Without both, the body or the latency is an account-enumeration oracle.
- **`algorithms=["HS256"]` is pinned.** Without that allowlist the classic `alg: none` forgery mints admin tokens at will — there is a test that attempts exactly that forgery.
- **`token_version` gives per-user revocation** without a session store. A ban that waits for a token to expire is not a ban. Logout and admin revoke both verified to kill a live token.
- **Free-tier limits are applied to the query**, not the response. Verified: free user asking for 20 gets **5** with `limit_reached: true` and an empty page 2; premium gets 20.

## A test failure that was actually a design inconsistency

One test reached the real database. The obvious fix was a test fixture; the real cause was that the feed handler built `UserRepository` inline while every other handler received it injected, contrary to ADR-0002. Fixed the handler — the test then passed with no scaffolding at all, which is the signal the fix was in the right place.

## Quality gates

**144 tests** (was 95) · `ruff` clean · `mypy --strict` clean across 64 files · `alembic check` clean.

Closes BL-012, BL-014, BL-015, BL-016. Rewrites BL-002 and BL-013. Opens BL-028 (no registration), BL-029 (no password reset), BL-030 (no login rate limiting), BL-031, BL-032.

BL-028 and BL-029 are direct costs of choosing passwords over OAuth — Google would have owned both problems entirely.

author: nipeno
body:
## What

Two things, both aimed at support:

**Logging.** The add-on wrote nothing to `ReShade.log`. Every line about it came from ReShade itself (`Registered add-on "NightZoom FPS Limiter" v… using ReShade API version 11.`), which proves the DLL loaded but says nothing about whether initialisation succeeded or the `present` callback ever ran — the exact gap behind the "installed it, no overlay" reports. `nz_log()` now wraps `reshade::log_message`:

| Level | Line |
| --- | --- |
| INFO | `NightZoom FPS Limiter v<ver> loaded - cap 60 FPS, wait path: high-resolution timer\|sleep fallback` |
| INFO | `Effect runtime initialised (device API: D3D11)` |
| INFO | `First frame presented; limiter enabled\|disabled` (once per process) |
| WARN | high-resolution timer unavailable, logo PNG decode failure, logo texture creation failure |
| DEBUG | config read, runtime destroy, unload |

ReShade has no runtime log level — `ReShadeLogMessage` (`source/addon.cpp`) prefixes the add-on name and passes every message straight to `reshade::log::message`, so DEBUG lines are written too and the level is severity labelling rather than a filter. That's why nothing is logged per frame — `on_present` gains a single relaxed atomic-exchange branch and is otherwise untouched.

**Overlay placement.** The window now opens at a deliberate size/position on first run (320 wide, auto height, at 45%/20% of the screen so it clears ReShade's left-hand dock column), set with `ImGuiCond_FirstUseEver`.

Worth recording: ReShade *already* persists this window's position, size, collapsed state and dock slot — it sets `io.IniFilename = nullptr` and pipes ImGui's settings handlers into `ReShade.ini` under `[OVERLAY] Window=` / `Docking=`, **keyed by the window title**. That saved entry overrides `FirstUseEver`, so a user's own placement always wins, and renaming the overlay would discard everyone's layout (there's now a code comment saying so).

Docking the window into ReShade's own Home/Add-ons/Settings tab group by default is *not* possible from an add-on: ReShade builds that layout with `DockBuilder*`, which is ImGui-internal and absent from `ReShadeGetImGuiFunctionTable()`, and the node IDs it generates aren't derivable. Users can still drag it in themselves, and that sticks. Documented in BUILDING.md so it isn't re-attempted.

## Testing

Not merged until a real FiveM smoke test passes:

- [x] CI compiles — [run 30713401253](https://github.com/Nipeno/nightzoom-fps-limiter/actions/runs/30713401253), artifact `NZ-FPS-Limiter`
- [x] `ReShade.log` shows the load line, the runtime-init line with the right device API, and the first-present line
- [x] no unexpected WARN (a logo WARN means the placeholder box is showing — visually checkable)
- [x] toggling the checkbox writes nothing to the log (a healthy launch is five lines, then quiet)
- [x] fresh install (or `[OVERLAY] Window=` deleted from `ReShade.ini`) → window appears at the new default spot
- [x] move/resize/dock it, restart → comes back where it was left
- [x] cap still holds at 60.0 FPS

author: monkius-maximus
body:
> **Stacks on #6.** Base is `claude/open-world-game-ui-vision-nk6tw6`, so this diff shows only the new work. GitHub retargets to `main` automatically once #6 merges.

Three artifacts described the same game in different words — the reimagined prototype in English, the open-world mockups in Portuguese, and this codebase somewhere between. This resolves the conflicts rather than picking a winner, and adds the pieces that genuinely increment the simulation.

---

## 1. Language — the actual conflict

The rule, applied everywhere:

> **Identifiers stay in English. Everything the player reads is a key.**

The simulation never holds a sentence. `LifeActivity` carries `activity.sleep.name`; whether that draws as "Dormir" or "Sleep" is decided at draw time by `ILocalizer`. **pt-BR is the default locale and the source of truth**; `en` is the pivot so the code's identifiers have an obvious counterpart.

- Keys are built by `LocKeys`, never written as literals, so a rename is a compile error instead of a silently missing string.
- A key with no translation renders **as the key** — `activity.shower.name` on a button is unmistakable in playtest; a blank button is not.
- The catalogue lives in Core rather than as a Godot resource, because a dictionary needs no engine and being there makes **key coverage unit-testable**: every producible key must resolve in every locale *directly*, and the locales must not drift apart. Both are pinned by test.

`EventDefinition.Title`/`Prompt` and `EventChoice.Label`/`Description` became derived keys, so no prose survives anywhere in the simulation.

## 2. Needs — four lists into one

| Source | Listed |
| --- | --- |
| First implementation | Energy, Nutrition, Fitness, Morale, Social, Focus |
| Open-world HUD mockup | Energia, Fome, Moral, Social, Higiene |
| Phone health app | Energia, Fome, Higiene, Sono, Estresse, Dor Muscular |
| Reimagined prototype | Energy, Sharpness, Morale, Injury Risk |

Folded into **eight** under four rules:

1. **Every gauge points the same way — 100 is good.** "Fome" and "Dor Muscular" are deficits that fill as things worsen; modelled as `Nutrition` and `MuscleCondition` so nothing has inverted polarity. Worth more than matching a mockup's noun.
2. **"Sono" folds into `Energy`.** Both are answered by the same act and would move together forever. Two gauges the player can never separate teach a decision that does not exist.
3. **"Estresse" and "Injury Risk" are not needs.** You cannot rest a stress bar — you rest the things that cause it. Both are computed in `WellbeingSnapshot`.
4. **"Sharpness" is `Focus`.**

**`MuscleCondition` is the one that changes the simulation rather than the UI.** A player can be well rested and still sore, and it is soreness — not tiredness — that turns a heavy training week into a torn hamstring. Training now buys conditioning with rest, food, **soreness and hygiene**, and soreness is the second-largest input to `InjuryRisk` after conditioning. The cross-effect graph grew to five edges (`Nutrition→Fitness`, `Energy→Focus`, `Social→Morale`, `Hygiene→Morale`, `MuscleCondition→Fitness`) so a bad week compounds instead of degrading linearly.

`Hygiene` needed an activity to service it, which surfaced a general rule now pinned by test: **every need must be raisable by some activity, for both career roles.** A gauge the player cannot service is not a system, it is a scold.

## 3. Test world, with the City Searcher seam

Per your call — the real world comes from the tool in its own sprint; this is the placeholder that makes the merge an import rather than a rewrite.

`TestWorldGazetteer` is a small fictional city (Verith) that copies the tool's conventions exactly: same id scheme (`test.verith#apartamento`), same hierarchy levels (`Region → … → Venue`). Everything reaches it through `IWorldGazetteer` and **nothing anywhere names a place**, so swapping the implementation is the entire integration.

The join with the life-sim is `VenueCategory`: an activity declares the *kind* of venue it needs (`physio` needs `Medical`) and any venue of that category hosts it — so activities are never re-authored per location, and mapping the gazetteer's free-text `detail.type` onto a category is the whole content step. This is also what turns a menu of buttons into a reason to go somewhere.

New **`docs/WORLD_INTEGRATION.md`** records the ordered merge sequence, what the gazetteer carries that this port deliberately does not yet (`detail.actions` → events/quests, `lens` → competition binding, `archetypeId` → procedural flavour, `layout` → routed travel), and the one open question to settle before the import: **how much world a save carries.**

## 4. Contextual input and the phone

Adapted from the reimagined prototype's platform map, which had the right abstraction. Screens declare **verbs**, never buttons; `GameInput` resolves the glyph for whichever device was last touched (keyboard / Xbox / PlayStation, whose shapes are also colour-coded).

`Esc` and `Start` both map to `Menu`, and `Menu` also means "close whatever is open" — so one key steps back out of a phone app, then closes the phone, then opens the quick menu. Actions are registered into `InputMap` **in code**: the editor's serialised `InputEvent` blobs are unreviewable in a diff.

The phone is the quick menu, opening on `P` / `Y` / `△`, with three apps — Saúde (the same `NeedsPanel` the scene uses, bound to the same service), Agenda, Mapa. One rule, and it is the one that matters: **every app is a view onto a system that already exists.** The phone must never become the place where state secretly lives.

## 5. Art direction — a correction

Recorded in `docs/UI_DESIGN_SYSTEM.md`, correcting an earlier framing in #6 that called for "2D".

Project Zomboid is a **3D** game: since build 41 its characters and objects are 3D models, many deliberately *thin* — flattened on the Z axis so they read as sprites — rendered into a fixed isometric camera and textured in a pixel-art idiom. It reads as 2D at a fraction of the cost of a free-camera 3D game while keeping real lighting, occlusion and reusable models.

**That is the target** — not photoreal (the mockup is a mood board whose fidelity would consume the project), and not flat 2D either, since those assets would not carry over if the camera ever moves. Nothing in the design system assumes 2D: the tokens and controls are `Control` nodes on a `CanvasLayer` and compose over a `Node2D` or `Node3D` root identically.

---

## Verification

- `dotnet build SoccerDreamGame.sln` — **0 errors, 0 warnings**, including the Godot project.
- `dotnet test` — **196 passing** (was 165; +31).
- New coverage: localisation key coverage and locale drift, the world seam (id scheme, venue gating, every-need-raisable for both roles), and the reconciled needs (Hygiene→Morale and MuscleCondition→Fitness cross-effects, soreness driving injury risk independently of rest, Stress falling only because its causes were serviced).

## Still open

- **The quick menu itself is not built.** `Esc`/`Start` currently only dismisses the phone; the verb and prompt exist, the menu does not.
- **Carried over from #6, unchanged:** `SyncFormMood` still has no call site in game code (proven by test, not yet invoked — `GameBootstrap` never loads a `Player` aggregate); activity costs are logged but never charged, since `IEconomyService` has no implementation; and there is still no UI path to start a Manager career, though `CareerRole` is fully persisted and honoured.
- **Never run in the Godot editor** — no binary in this environment. Everything is compile-verified, which catches API errors but not layout or anchoring bugs.

author: cao825
body:
Turns the auto-triage rung on. The rung itself is unchanged — it shipped default-off deliberately ("a rung that spends unsupervised is opted into, never shipped on") and this is the opt-in.

## What the daemon will do with it

The rung is already running and only the flag is stopping it. That is measured, not inferred: the ledger carries 99 `auto_triage.skipped` lines, every one reading `auto-triage disabled (policy.autoTriage.enabled=false)`, the most recent minutes before this branch was cut. That reason comes from the FIRST guard in `decideAutoTriage`, so the hook is wired, the idle branch is entered, and nothing downstream is blocking.

Once enabled it fires only from the daemon's idle branch — not on cadence — where "nothing dispatchable, nothing in flight" is already known. Three bounds gate it: the flag, a 60-minute minimum interval measured from the newest recorded fire, and a rolling cap of 4 per 24 hours. It also refuses while the shared triage lock is held by a live process, and fails closed on an unreadable marker. The fire is recorded BEFORE the triage spawns, so a crash mid-run costs a skipped period rather than authorising an immediate retry.

Against live state right now the marker is absent and the lock is unheld, so both pacing bounds pass on the first idle tick. There are 67 feedback entries at status new; the deterministic pick is the oldest, `fb-1784433603527-48134e` from 2026-07-19 — a report that the drain retry banner overlaps the status pill on narrow viewports. Oldest-first is stable, so a fire that fails and retries next period picks the same entry rather than skipping ahead.

This does not reach the running daemon until the canonical checkout pulls the merge — the rung reads the policy file fresh on every check, but from the install path.

## The test change, and why it is here

Flipping the flag broke `test/auto-triage-wiring.test.ts`, and the failure was a real defect in the test rather than a signal about the rung.

That test was titled "the wired hook refuses to fire with the policy flag ABSENT" and asserted an unconditional refusal. But its fixture writes a config and a task list and no policy file at all, while the hook it drives reads the policy from the repo root resolved off the test process's own working directory. So it was reading the CHECKED-IN policy and really asserting "the shipped default is false". It passed by coincidence of that value, and a genuine flag flip broke it — a test failing for the one thing it should not care about.

The fix keeps the file's whole reason for existing intact. This suite exists because PR #1066 shipped a consumer with no producer and eighteen direct-call tests passed anyway; every test here drives the real command and asserts on the real deps. So the replacement still drives the real wiring, and pins what is actually invariant: the wired hook DERIVES its answer from the policy file. It asserts both directions — flag off means refuse and say the flag is why; flag on means it must never claim to be disabled, while still allowing the legitimate refusals for a held lock or an empty candidate list. It now passes with the flag set either way, which is verified below.

The absent-block default the old title claimed to cover is genuinely worth testing, so it is asserted directly against the policy loader, where that semantics actually lives — a policy file with the block stripped out must load as disabled.

## Acceptance

- the wired hook obeys the checked-in flag in both directions rather than a hardcoded expectation | unit test: the wired hook's decision tracks the checked-in policy
- a policy file with no autoTriage block still loads as disabled | unit test: a policy.yaml with no autoTriage block loads as disabled
- the rung's producer is still wired into the deps the daemon receives | unit test: daemonCommand actually WIRES checkAutoTriage into the deps it hands runDaemon
- the decoupled wiring test exists on this branch | grep: THE FLAG IS OBEYED THROUGH THE WIRING in test/auto-triage-wiring.test.ts

## Verification

tsc clean, commitlint clean. lint-plan reports 313 checked and 193 failing, which is main's own baseline.

Scoped suites: auto-triage-wiring 7 of 7 (was 6, one added), auto-triage-rung 18 of 18, policy 45 of 45, daemon 87 of 87.

The decoupling proof: the same test file was run with the flag set to false and to true. Seven of seven both times. The old assertion would still fail on this branch, so this repairs a coupling rather than deleting an inconvenient check — against live state the wired decision with the flag on is fire true on `fb-1784433603527-48134e`.

Proofs were run under test-name-pattern, each matching one passing test after excluding the wrapper by full path, with a zero-match control returning 0. The grep proof used the executor's own invocation rather than a fixed-string matcher: 0 hits and exit 1 against main, 1 hit and exit 0 here, metacharacter-free against a NUL-free file.

body:
Ships tycho #117.

**The bug a real user hit.** The setup screen tells every new member to run `./tycho-client -conf tycho.yaml`; the binary answered with a usage string demanding `-key key.pem`. That file is the shared fleet interop RSA key the Seestar's `get_verify_str` handshake requires — deliberately not in the repo, and something a member who signed up an hour ago cannot obtain. So onboarding stopped dead at step 3.

**Served, not shipped.** `GET /v1/device-key`, authenticated with the per-scope secret, refused for a revoked scope. The client holds it **in memory only** and refetches each start. `TestEnrolMode_DeviceKeyNeverLeaks` runs a full enrolment and asserts the PEM appears in neither `tycho.yaml`, nor any buffer file, nor any rendered TUI frame.

Bundling it would have put the key in a published artifact, identical for everyone and unrotatable without a release. Serving it means one copy, rotatable centrally the day ZWO changes it in firmware — the endpoint already takes a `firmware` parameter (ignored for now) as the seam for that.

Honest limit, stated in the code as well as here: anyone who signs up can obtain this key. It is access-controlled provisioning, not secrecy.

**No new secret.** `DEVICE_INTEROP_KEY_PEM` reads `tycho-config/see_start_pem` — the same material the agent already mounts at `KEY_PATH`. The gateway refuses to start if it collides with any other configured value.

author: joseph-cursio
body:
Prompted by finding that `HomomorphismTemplate` — a shipped template with a carefully argued doc and a full exclusion list — fires **zero times**. If one template can be dead without anyone noticing, how many others are?

Eight corpora, ~55,000 scanned functions, rows per template against the 39 declared `templateName`s.

## The distribution

| rows | templates |
|---:|---|
| **0** | `diff-disjointness`, `homomorphism`, `involution`, `multiplicative-homomorphism`, `partition`, `selection-subset` |
| 1–2 | `composition`, `caseiterable-case-coverage`, `caseiterable-key-injectivity`, `override-precedence`, `invariant-preservation`, `bulk-incremental-agreement` |
| 48–1,598 | `commutativity` … `idempotence` |

**6 of 39 never fire. 12 of 39 produce ≤2 rows.** And `idempotence` + `predicate` + `round-trip` are **2,724 of 4,102 rows — 66% of all output**, which is the quantitative form of "the tool says the generic thing when it has nothing specific to say."

## Why it went unnoticed

**A dead template and a correctly-silent one produce identical output.** The catalog's posture is high precision / low recall, so silence is the expected state and nobody investigates it. This is the four-kinds-of-silence problem the study built for *corpora*, turned on our own catalog.

## One cause diagnosed; the other five are not the same story

`HomomorphismTemplate`'s gate is `parameters.count == 1 && isArrayShaped(param.typeText)` — a **free function** `[T] -> Int`. Nobody writes `func count(_ xs: [T]) -> Int` in Swift; they write `var count: Int`. **It was built for a shape the language doesn't use.**

The member form has population — `Array`, `BitArray`, `RigidArray`, `IndexPath`, `SyntaxCollection`, `BigString.UnicodeScalarView` — with `String` and `BigString` excluded on the template's *own* existing reasoning (grapheme count isn't additive across a combining-character boundary).

**`InvolutionTemplate` does NOT share that cause** — it already handles a member form. So the six zeros aren't one bug repeated, and each needs its own diagnosis before anyone fixes them as a batch.

## Process

The census belongs in the road-test routine. One `discover` run per corpus, and it answers a question no existing mode does: `metrics` aggregates *decisions* about surfaced rows, `--stats-only` reports one corpus, and neither can see a template that reaches nothing everywhere.

It also reframes "add a template" as a decision with an ongoing cost: 15% of what's been added so far is inert, and the inertness was invisible.

Docs only.

author: ianwremmel-ai-agent
body:
The pre-push skill review reviewed one file at a time. That made the gate unpassable by construction for any change large enough to matter.

## The failure

git opens its connection to the remote *before* running `pre-push`, then holds it idle until the hook returns. Hook wall-clock is therefore charged against the remote's idle timeout. GitHub closes the connection somewhere under seven minutes; git then dies of SIGPIPE writing the pack — exit 141, with no message beyond ssh's `Connection to github.com closed by remote host` buried mid-report.

One review takes 70–90 s (measured: 69 s for a 120-word file). Serially, five or more changed skill files outlives the connection. On #180's branch — 7 skill files — the hook took ~10 minutes and **every** push failed, including runs where all seven files returned `VERDICT: pass`. The verdict was irrelevant; the push could never complete.

Reproduced independently of the reviewer, with a dummy hook:

```
$ printf '#!/usr/bin/env sh\ncat >/dev/null\nsleep 420\nexit 0\n' > "$H/pre-push"
$ git -c core.hooksPath="$H" push --dry-run origin HEAD:refs/heads/scratch
exit=141
Connection to github.com closed by remote host.

$ GIT_SSH_COMMAND='ssh -o ServerAliveInterval=60' git -c core.hooksPath="$H" push --dry-run ...
exit=0
```

A keepalive papers over it. Not outliving the connection in the first place is the actual fix.

## The change

Reviews are independent — `review(file)` only reads its own file — so they go through a worker pool (`mapWithConcurrency`, cap 8). Workers pull from a shared cursor rather than running fixed batches, so one slow file never idles the others behind a barrier.

Reports are now buffered and written in a single call when each reviewer finishes, rather than streamed as they arrive. Concurrent streaming would interleave chunks from eight agents and shred every report.

Kept one file per reviewer rather than handing the whole set to one agent: parallel wall-clock is the slowest single file, the `VERDICT:`-as-last-line contract and the `failed[]` file list survive untouched, and `.claude/agents/skill-reviewer.md` is written for a single file.

## Result

Same 7-file range, before and after:

| | wall clock |
| --- | --- |
| serial | ~10 min (push always failed) |
| concurrent | 1 m 36 s |

Verified the reports survive: 7 blocks, 7 `VERDICT:` lines, one per block, no interleaving, and the summary named the right blocking file.

## Residual

A change touching enough skill files to need several waves could still approach the limit — 8 at a time with the 300 s per-file cap is 10 min worst case at 24 files. If that shows up, the next step is a total-time budget that fails open rather than stranding the push.

## Verification

`npm run lint`, `npm run typecheck`, `npm test` (200 pass, 4 new covering input-order preservation, the concurrency ceiling, cursor-not-batch scheduling, and the empty list).

author: bulent2k2
body:
## What

The anchor-interval pull model (#523 / PR #539) computes a per-segment **flat-optimum interval** `[pull_lo, pull_hi]` (connected wirelength is minimized over it — NUTS may slide the segment across it for free) plus the **|slopes|** just outside it (`pull_f_lo`/`pull_f_hi`, the WL paid per unit of slide below/above). But both human-facing inspection displays still printed only the *derived scalar* `pull=<dir>(net_pull)` — so on a WL-flat segment (net_pull 0) the entire interval was invisible and the feature looked absent.

Both surfaces now append `opt=[lo..hi] f=lo/hi`:
- `dump_topologies --conn` (`reports.py`)
- the Topology Explorer segment info bar (`viz_explorer/analysis.py`)

Example — a symmetric star where every stub sits WL-flat reads `pull=none(0)` on the scalar yet now shows its real optima:
```
seg0  H M4  along[199,601] perp=400  slide=[320..480]=160  pull=none(0)  opt=[300..500] f=6/6
seg2  V M5  along[400,500] perp=400  slide=[301..499]=198  pull=none(0)  opt=[101..699] f=1/1
```

## Design notes

- **Display-only** — no logic or behavior change; the derived scalar still leads for continuity, the interval is purely additive.
- `opt=` is **omitted when the optimum is flat everywhere** (the `INT_MIN..INT_MAX` sentinel — no anchor constrains the slide), so unconstrained segments stay terse. One-sided-infinite optima render `-inf`/`+inf`.
- The formatter `_fmt_pull_opt` is kept as **independent copies** in the two display layers (no viz→session coupling — matches the codebase's existing per-layer formatting duplication, e.g. the slide/`free` rendering); a test pins them equal.

## Tests

`test/tests/test_pull_optimum_display.py` — 5 cases: the `--conn` surface, the explorer info bar (`_seg_conn_line`), formatter agreement across the two layers, flat-everywhere omission, and one-sided-infinite rendering. Adjacent pull/conn/explorer suites stay green.

Docs: the CLAUDE.md `dump_topologies` row and `interval_pull_model.md` now describe the surfaced interval.

body:
## Problems

**1. The standard wash was quoted at the cheapest package's price.** `PackagesEditor` auto-sets `operators.base_price_cents` to `Math.min(...activePackagePrices)`, and the resident-facing rate fell back to it. So "Standard wash" showed a number nobody chose — it just tracked whichever package was cheapest.

**2. The operator was told almost nothing about the job.** The booking email carried `colour make model` and a payout. The parking spot, unit, plate, building address and access notes were all one join away and never sent.

**3. One-off bookings were invisible until the day they happened.** `/operator/bookings` existed but wasn't in the operator nav. The only nav-reachable view was Today, which queries `scheduled_for = today` — a booking made for next Tuesday couldn't be seen until Tuesday.

## Changes

**Per-building pricing** — new `partnerships.standard_wash_price_cents`, set by the operator per building from a price editor on `/operator/buildings` (with the current fallback shown when unset). `lib/building-price.ts` centralises resolution — package price → building rate → operator rate — so `bookings/create`, `promo/preview` and the booking form can't drift apart. Falls back to `contracts.price_per_wash_cents` for partnerships predating the column, then to the operator rate, so nothing changes until an operator sets a price. Promo previews now also account for the selected package, which they previously ignored.

**Job details to the operator** — the booking email now carries address, unit, spot + floor, plate, access notes, package, add-ons and resident notes. The same details go into the ICS invite body so the calendar entry stands on its own without opening the app. The resident sees the identical summary in the booking panel before paying, with a link to fix their spot/access, and can add free-text notes (`bookings.resident_notes`) for anything not already on their profile.

**Operator nav** — added Bookings.

## Migration

`supabase/migrations/0052_building_wash_price_and_booking_notes.sql` adds `partnerships.standard_wash_price_cents` and `bookings.resident_notes`. Both nullable and additive.

Deployment ordering matters, and `0051` from the previous PR must be applied too. `booking-confirm.ts` deliberately reads `resident_notes` in its own query rather than the main select — it runs on the paid-booking path, and a deploy landing ahead of the migration must still send both emails and build the crew roster.

## Verification

`tsc --noEmit` clean, `npm run build` exits 0. The two `Supabase admin env vars missing` build lines are pre-existing — identical count on a stashed baseline.

Not exercised against a live database, Stripe, or Resend: the per-building price, the enriched operator email and the ICS body are all unverified end-to-end.

author: ameenahassan421
body:
Docs only — no code, no behaviour change. Records what a live egress check actually found, so the next session does not have to rediscover it.

## What was verified

Every allowlisted host answers on 443. A 401/403/404 is a pass: it means a real server replied, not that the tunnel failed.

| host | result |
| --- | --- |
| `api.supabase.com` | 404 on `/`, and `npm run supabase:admin -- show` returned live project config — authenticated end-to-end |
| `ttasiwxeqerhsztxjxip.supabase.co` | 401 `No API key found in request` from `/auth/v1/health` |
| `api.vercel.com` | 403 `missing an authentication token` from `/v2/user` |
| `api.resend.com` | 401 `Missing API Key` from `/emails` |
| `api.github.com` | 200 from `/rate_limit` |

Enforcement was confirmed to be real rather than assumed: `example.com` and `api.openai.com` are refused with `403` on CONNECT, and the proxy logs the denial under `recentRelayFailures`.

## Two findings the doc did not cover

**Host matching is exact, not by domain.** `api.supabase.com` being allowed does not make `supabase.com` allowed. The apex domains of all three providers — `supabase.com`, `vercel.com`, `resend.com` — are denied.

**Port 5432 does not traverse the proxy, and fails deceptively.** The local proxy answers `HTTP/1.1 200 Connection Established` to a CONNECT on *any* non-443 port, for *any* host, allowlisted or not. `example.com:9999` gets the same 200 as the database. Only port 443 is actually policy-checked.

Past that 200, no bytes flow in either direction, nothing is recorded in `recentRelayFailures`, and the client hangs until it times out. Probing with a Postgres `SSLRequest` packet through the tunnel — direct and pooler, 5432 and 6543 — got zero bytes back in every case.

The failure mode matters more than the fact: a session that probes with CONNECT alone reads the 200 as success, concludes Postgres is reachable, and then stalls on a handshake that will never complete. The doc now says a 200 on a non-443 port is not evidence of anything, and points at the data API on 443 instead.

## Noticed but not changed

`supabase:admin -- show` surfaced live auth config that conflicts with `CLAUDE.md`. Out of scope for this branch and it mutates a production project, so it is flagged here rather than fixed:

- `mailer_otp_length: 8`, but `CLAUDE.md` mandates a 6-digit code
- both email templates lack `{{ .Token }}`, which per `CLAUDE.md` makes sign-in impossible
- `site_url: http://localhost:3000`, not the production URL; `uri_allow_list` empty
- no custom SMTP, which Supabase requires before template writes take effect

## Test plan

No code touched. `npm run format:check` passes.
